summary.text: A 67-year-old woman presented with acute continuous vertigo, nausea and vomiting and was admitted for substantial truncal ataxia and inability to sit without support. Two serial brain MRIs were normal. An otoneurology consult found low-amplitude downbeat nystagmus, direction-changing horizontal nystagmus in lateral gaze, saccadic pursuit and a normal head impulse test.

CSF showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (98 /mm^(3)) and elevated protein (106 mg/dL). CT identified an ovarian mass and CA-125 was significantly elevated. She received IV methylprednisolone and five daily plasma exchanges, then complete surgical excision yielding ovarian carcinoma. The paraneoplastic panel was positive for PCA-1 antibodies.

After surgery, carboplatin was followed by partial improvement and resolution of her AVS despite persistent DBN, but gait stayed unstable and she used a wheelchair. Tumor later recurred with systemic metastases, she withdrew life-prolonging treatment and entered hospice. Autopsy showed extensive cerebellar folia atrophy, Purkinje cell loss and cerebral metastases without active inflammation.

summary.text: A 68-year-old man was transferred from an outside hospital with acute continuous vertigo, nausea, vomiting, oscillopsia and ataxia with worsening ability to stand over the week before admission. Examination on arrival showed subtle downbeat nystagmus with a direction-changing horizontal component in lateral gaze, poor visual fixation, unilaterally decreased VOR gain with a corrective saccade after the left head impulse, and inability to sit without support. Head MRI was normal.

CSF showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (50 cells/1 mm^(3)) and mildly elevated protein (54.5 mg/dL). Oncologic workup found a distal esophageal mass and biopsy showed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. The paraneoplastic panel was positive for anti-PCA-1 antibodies. High-dose steroids and plasma exchange were begun.

Nausea and vomiting subsided with medication but the downbeat nystagmus increased in intensity. In the rehabilitation unit 2 weeks later he continued to deteriorate rapidly with progressive confusion and a truncal tremor/myorhythmia syndrome. He elected no further treatment and later transitioned to hospice care.

summary.text: An 80-year-old previously healthy woman was transferred from an outside hospital for a one-month history of rapidly progressive dysarthria and ataxia, after initial sudden vertigo, weakness, nausea and vomiting that improved. Past history included ulcerative colitis and remote hysterectomy with unilateral oophorectomy. Examination showed downbeat nystagmus, delayed vertical saccades, scanning dysarthria and moderate ataxia of all extremities, with a normal head impulse test.

Serial brain MRIs were unremarkable. CSF showed elevated protein (118 mg/dL) and lymphocytic pleocytosis, and PCA Ab type-1 was positive. Before transfer she received high-dose solumedrol alternating with IV immunoglobulin without consistent benefit. CA-125 was elevated at 183.6 U/mL, and PET showed hypermetabolic lymph nodes with biopsy of non-small cell carcinoma of unknown primary.

In hospital she received plasma exchange alternating with methylprednisolone, with minimal recovery but no further functional decline after plasmapheresis was initiated. She then started initial maintenance rituximab. Because of severe persistent disability, life-prolonging treatments were discontinued following the patient and family directive to transition to hospice.
